chunks: Ibn Mahbub, from Jamil ibn Salih, from al-Fudayl ibn Yasar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

'What prevents the trader among you, the one busy in his market, when he returns to his house, from not sleeping until he recites a chapter from the Quran, so that for every verse he recites, ten good deeds would be written for him, and ten evil deeds would be erased from him?'

key_terms.التاجر: Trader/merchant — the Imam addresses this teaching specifically to those engaged in commerce, indicating this ruling applies to all busy people
key_terms.حسنات: Good deeds recorded in one's account; the multiplied reward (ten per verse) emphasizes the immense spiritual value of Quran recitation
key_terms.سورة من القرآن: A chapter from the Quran — not necessarily a long chapter; even a short surah like al-Ikhlas suffices
key_terms.سيئات: Evil deeds erased from the record — the dual benefit of earning rewards and having sins removed

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about reciting Quran before sleeping?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) addresses a rhetorical question to traders who spend their days occupied in commerce: there is no valid excuse for them not to recite at least one chapter of the Quran before sleeping. The Imam highlights the immense spiritual reward — ten good deeds recorded and ten sins erased per verse — making even a short recitation enormously beneficial. This teaching was particularly directed at early Muslim merchants in Medina and Kufa who would return exhausted from their markets, and the Imam's rhetorical framing ('what prevents you?') carries a gentle yet firm exhortation to prioritize Quran recitation even amid the demands of worldly livelihood.
